A sentence has been given in Direct or Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect or Direct speech.
He said, "My parents take a walk every day."
optA: He said that his parents took a walk every day.
optB: He said that his parents might be taking a walk every day.
optC: He said that his parents were taking a walk every day.
optD: He advised that his parents should take a walk every day.
context: In the following questions, a sentence has been given in Direct or Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect or Direct speech.
solution: The reporting verb 'said' is in the past tense, so the reported clause backshifts one step: the simple present 'take' becomes the simple past 'took'. The first-person possessive 'My' shifts to the third person 'his' to match the reporter's point of view. Leaving 'take' unchanged makes no backshift at all, while the continuous and modal versions add a sense of ongoing action or possibility that the original statement never carried, and 'advised ... should' converts a plain statement into a piece of advice. Matches option A.

stem: It can be inferred from the passage that this year's fire in Australia is mostly a result of:
optB: An accidental spark in the jungle
optC: A result of an extraordinarily hot and dry spell
optD: A deliberate attempt to put the forests on fire
context: Since September, at least 25 people have died and thousands have been made homeless. Every state and territory in Australia has experienced fires this summer. But the biggest fires burn along stretches of the eastern and southern coast, where most of the population lives. This includes areas around sydney and Adelaide. More than 6.3 million hectares (63,000 sq km or 15.6 million acres) have been burned so far - one Hectare is roughly the size of a sports field. To put that in perspective, around 800,000 Hectares were engulfed in a bush fire in 2018 in California. Australia has always experienced bushfires - it has a "fire season". But this year they are a lot worse than normal. Fires are usually caused by lightning strikes or accidentally by a spark - but some fires are also started deliberately. This year, a natural weather phenomenon known as the 'Indian Ocean Dipole' has meant a hot, dry spell across the country. This year, Australia twice set a new temperature record: an average maximum of \(41.9^{\circ}C\) was recorded on 18 December. That comes on top of a long period of drought. Scientists have long warned that this hotter, drier climate will contribute to fires becoming more frequent and more intense. The more extreme weather patterns and higher temperatures increase the risk of bushfires and allow them to spread faster and wider. Fire fighters are spraying water and fire retardant from planes and helicopters as well as from the ground. But fighting bushfires is extremely difficult and often authorities have to focus on just stopping the Spread, rather than putting the fire out. The spread can for instance be best contained by digging earth boundaries to stop the flames from spreading. The priority is saving lives. Professional fire fighters are the first in line to battle the flames, but they are outnumbered by the thousands of volunteers. Three of them have died. There's also help coming from abroad: the US, Canada and New Zealand have sent firefighters to help. Australia's police, military and navy are involved in rescue and evacuation efforts. While people can flee the fires and are being evacuated, if need be, the flames are devastating wildlife in the affected areas. One study estimated that half a billion animals have died in New South wales alone. Zookeepers take animals home to save them from fire, but the fires don't only kill animals directly, they also destroy the habitat, leaving the survivors vulnerable even when the fires have gone. So, the true scale of loss isn't yet clear. Experts say more than 100,000 cows and sheep may also have been lost, which is devastating for farmers. Each state runs its own emergency operation, but Prime Minister Scott Morrison has promised better funding for fire-fighting and payouts for volunteer firefighters, and an additional 2 billion Australian dollars (1.4 billion US dollars; 1 billion pounds) for the recovery. But the national government has come under strong criticism from its opponents that it has not been doing enough against climate change. The country is one of the world's biggest per capita greenhouse gas emitters but under international agreements it has committed itself to reduction targets.
solution: The passage carefully separates the usual causes of bushfires - lightning strikes, an accidental spark, and fires started deliberately - from what made this particular season different. For this year it names the Indian Ocean Dipole, which produced a hot, dry spell across the country, a national temperature record set twice, and a long preceding drought. Lightning and sparks are therefore how fires generally start, not why this season was so much worse than normal. Matches option C.

stem: The Tornadoes are very strong tropical cyclones originating in:

optD: Equality before law and equal protection of the laws
solution: Article 14 reads that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws. stem: The most suitable metal for making permanent magnets is:
solution: Permanent magnets need high retentivity, so the material keeps its magnetism once the field is removed, and high coercivity, so a stray field cannot wipe it out. Steel has both. Soft iron magnetises very strongly but loses it the instant the current stops, which is exactly what an electromagnet wants and a permanent magnet does not, while copper and aluminium are not ferromagnetic at all. stem: The depth d at which the value of acceleration due to gravity becomes 1/\(n\) times the value at the surface, is [R = radius of the earth]
solution: Inside the earth the acceleration due to gravity falls linearly with depth, \(g_{d} = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)\). Setting \(g_{d} = \frac{g}{n}\) gives \(1 - \frac{d}{R} = \frac{1}{n}\), so \(\frac{d}{R} = \frac{n-1}{n}\) and \(d = R\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)\). The tempting choices assume an inverse-square fall, which is how \(g\) behaves with height but not with depth. Matches option B.

stem: An object is placed at 20 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image formed by the mirror is
optA: Real and at 20 cm from the mirror
optB: Virtual and at 20 cm from the mirror
optC: Virtual and at 20/3 cm from the mirror
optD: Real and at 20/3 cm from the mirror
solution: Apply \(\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}\) with \(u = -20\) cm and, for a convex mirror, \(f = +10\) cm. Then \(\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{3}{20}\), giving \(v = \frac{20}{3}\) cm. The positive sign places the image behind the mirror, so it is virtual, erect and diminished. Since a convex mirror can never form a real image of a real object, both real choices can be discarded before any arithmetic is done. Matches option C.

stem: The displacement-time graph of a particle acted upon by a constant force is
optD: any curve depending upon initial conditions
solution: Constant force means constant acceleration, and with constant acceleration the displacement follows \(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^{2}\). Displacement is quadratic in time, so the graph is a parabola; a straight line would require zero acceleration and therefore zero force. The suggestion that the shape depends on the initial conditions is tempting, but a different starting velocity only shifts and tilts the same curve, and the quadratic term set by the acceleration is always present. Matches option C.

3. Nanometer

Placed in increasing order that is angstrom, then nanometre, then micron, which is the sequence 1, 3, 2. The trap is reading the list in the order printed and assuming it is already sorted. Matches option C.

stem: To convert galvanometer into voltmeter one should connect:
optA: high resistance in series with galvanometer
optB: low resistance in series with galvanometer
optC: high resistance in parallel with galvanometer
optD: low resistance in parallel with galvanometer
solution: The galvanometer coil takes only a very small current, so to read a potential difference it must be given a large resistance in series, which drops nearly all the applied voltage and lets only a tiny current through the coil. That series resistance also raises the total resistance of the instrument, which is what an ideal voltmeter needs so it does not disturb the circuit it is measuring. Putting a small resistance in parallel instead gives the shunt used to make an ammeter, which is the standard confusion here. Matches option A.
subject: Physics

stem: Two bodies of equal mass move with the velocity of 2\(\nu\) and 3\(\nu\), respectively. Then, the ratio of their kinetic energies is
solution: Kinetic energy is \(\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), so with equal masses the ratio of the energies is the ratio of the squares of the speeds: \((2\nu)^{2} : (3\nu)^{2} = 4 : 9\). Taking the plain ratio of the speeds instead of their squares gives the tempting wrong answer. Matches option A.
subject: Physics

stem: A current loop placed in a non-uniform magnetic field experiences
solution: In a uniform field the forces on opposite sides of the loop are equal and opposite, so they cancel and only a turning effect survives; that is why a motor coil rotates without drifting. If the field is non-uniform the forces on the two sides are no longer equal, so a net force appears as well, while the torque is still there in general. Whether that net force pulls or pushes depends on how the loop is oriented, so neither attraction nor repulsion can be named on its own. Matches option D.
subject: Physics

stem: Water is usually heated by
solution: Water is a poor conductor of heat, so heating a vessel from below works by convection: the warmed layer at the bottom expands, becomes less dense and rises, cooler water sinks to take its place, and the circulating current carries heat through the whole body of liquid. Conduction alone would leave the top cold, and radiation plays almost no part at these temperatures. Matches option B.

stem: What is the power of the lens, if the far point of a short-sighted eye is 200 cm?
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED D -> A. The same question is already in the bank keyed A; an independent derivation agrees with the bank. solution: The short-sighted eye cannot see beyond its far point, so the corrective lens must take an object at infinity and form its image exactly at that far point, 200 cm or 2 m in front of the eye. With the object at infinity the object term vanishes and \(\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} = -\frac{1}{2}\) per metre, so \(f = -2\) m and the power is \(P = \frac{1}{f} = -0.5\) dioptre. Myopia always needs a diverging lens, so every positive power in the list can be thrown out before the arithmetic even begins. Matches option A.

stem: 'Mirage' is a phenomenon due to
solution: On a hot road the air just above the surface is much hotter, and so optically rarer, than the air above it. Light from the sky travelling downwards bends further and further away from the normal as it crosses these layers, and once its angle of incidence passes the critical angle it is turned back upwards altogether, so the observer sees a patch of sky lying on the road and reads it as water. Refraction is the tempting choice because it is what bends the ray in the first place, but the ray is only returned to the eye by total internal reflection, and offering both in the same list is precisely what makes that the discriminator. Matches option C.

stem: The resistance of a wire is 10 \(\Omega\). If it is stretched ten times,
solution: Stretching a wire keeps its volume unchanged, so if the length becomes \(n\) times the original then the cross-section becomes \(\frac{1}{n}\) times, and resistance, being proportional to length divided by cross-sectional area, rises by a factor of \(n^{2}\). Here \(n = 10\), so the resistance goes from \(10\) \(\Omega\) to \(10 \times 10^{2} = 1000\) \(\Omega\). Multiplying by ten instead of by a hundred is the usual slip, because it forgets that the wire also gets thinner. Matches option D.

stem: The top of Lake is frozen as the atmospheric temperature is \(-10^{\circ}\text{C}\). The temperature at the bottom of the lake is most likely to be
solution: Water is densest at \(4^{\circ}\text{C}\). As a lake loses heat, water chilled to that temperature sinks and gathers at the bottom; cooling it further makes it lighter again, so the colder water stays on top and eventually freezes there. The bottom therefore settles at about \(4^{\circ}\text{C}\) and the fish survive under the ice, whatever the air above the surface is doing. Matches option C.

stem: Unit of conductance is ____
solution: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, and its SI unit is the siemens, equal to one reciprocal ohm and once called the mho for that reason. The ohm measures resistance itself, the dyne is a CGS unit of force and the volt measures potential difference. Matches option B.

stem: Orbit of a planet around a star is
solution: Kepler's first law states that every planet moves along an ellipse with the star at one focus. The circle is only the special case of zero eccentricity, which no real orbit has exactly, and a parabolic path is an escape trajectory that would never bring the body back. Matches option B.

stem:
Assertion : The value of acceleration due to gravity does not depend upon mass of the body on which force is applied.
Reason : Acceleration due to gravity is a constant quantity.

solution: The assertion is true. Since \(g = \frac{GM}{r^{2}}\), it is fixed by the mass of the earth and the distance from its centre, and the mass of the falling body cancels out, which is why a stone and a feather fall together in a vacuum. The reason is false, because \(g\) is not a constant at all: it falls with height, it falls with depth, and it is larger at the poles than at the equator. So a true assertion sits beside a false reason. Matches option C.

stem: An electric fuse works on the:
solution: The fuse is a short length of wire with high resistivity and a low melting point, placed in series with the circuit it protects. When the current rises past the rated value the heat produced, \(H = I^{2}Rt\), melts that wire and breaks the circuit, so the fuse depends squarely on the heating effect of current. The magnetic effect is what a miniature circuit breaker or a relay uses instead, which is the tempting alternative here, and neither chemical action nor light plays any part. Matches option D.

stem:
Consider the following statements
1. Pulmonary artery is the only vein in which the impure blood is circulated from heart to lungs.
2. Pulmonary vein is the only artery in which the pure blood is circulated from lungs to heart.
3. Deoxygenated blood is circulated in the arteries.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution: The first two statements describe the right vessels doing the right jobs. Blood low in oxygen leaves the heart for the lungs through the pulmonary artery, and oxygen-rich blood returns from the lungs to the heart through the pulmonary vein, and those two are the standing exceptions to the usual pattern. The third statement is wrong, because arteries as a class carry oxygenated blood, and only the pulmonary artery, together with the umbilical artery in a foetus, carries the deoxygenated kind. Note the loose wording of the first two, which call the pulmonary artery a vein and the pulmonary vein an artery: a vessel is named by whether it leads away from or towards the heart, never by the kind of blood inside it. Matches option C.
subject: Biology
reviewNote: [KEY CORRECTED A -> C. Two independent blind derivations, neither with sight of the key nor of the other, reached the same answer against it. This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints A. Basis: Statements 1 and 2 carry the two standard pulmonary-circulation facts (impure blood heart->lungs, pure blood lungs->heart) and are accepted as true; statement 3 is false, because arteries as a class carry oxygenated blood - the pulmonary (and umbilical) artery is the exception, not the rule. So 1 and 2 only. The discriminating statement is 3, and it is unambiguously false as a general claim: 'deoxygenated blood is circulated in the arteries' is exactly the misconception the pulmonary artery is famous for violating. That eliminates B and D and leaves A vs C, decided by whether statement 2 is true - it is (the pulmonary vein is the one vein carrying oxygenated blood, lungs->heart), so C. optB: the chain reacation in nuclear reactor is controlled.

solution: Both a reactor and a bomb run on the same fission chain reaction, so any statement denying a chain reaction in one of them is wrong at once. solution: The statement about energy has the two cases the wrong way round. solution: The first statement is wrong: a sulphur molecule is octatomic, \(\text{S}_{8}\), a puckered ring of eight atoms. stem: What happened when a hard boiled egg after shelling is immersed in saturated brine?
optD: It initially grows in size and then
solution: Saturated brine is strongly hypertonic to the egg, so water moves out of the egg's protein gel across its membrane by osmosis, travelling down the water-potential gradient from the egg into the salt solution. Losing water, the egg shrinks and its surface wrinkles. It would swell only in the opposite case, if it were put into pure water or another hypotonic solution, so there is no stage at which it first grows. Matches option A.

This is publisher practice material, not a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve; the book prints C. Basis: The egg shrinks: saturated brine is strongly hypertonic, so water leaves the egg by osmosis across the shell membrane. After shelling, the boiled egg is a water-rich mass bounded by a semi-permeable membrane. Saturated NaCl solution has a far higher solute concentration (lower water potential) than the egg's contents, so the net osmotic flow of water is outward and the egg loses volume. Boiling denatures the proteins but does not remove the water nor make the membrane freely permeable to Na+ and Cl-, so the osmotic gradient still operates. B is the hypotonic (distilled-water) outcome. Recorded here rather than silently: option D is printed truncated - 'It initially grows in size and then' - with its consequent clause missing.
